prompt: Four comments arrive on your pull request. What do you do first?
hint: The worst replies are written quickly.

choices.text: Reply to the harshest one straight away
choices.why: That is the reply most likely to be regretted.

choices.text: Read all four before answering any
choices.why: Right. One comment often makes sense next to another.

choices.text: Fix the nit, since it is the quickest
choices.why: The blocking comment comes first.

choices.text: Ask for a different reviewer
choices.why: Nothing yet suggests the review is unfair.

prompt: A reviewer left a comment without saying how serious it is. How should you treat it?
hint: When unsure, be safe and ask.

choices.text: As a nit you may ignore
choices.why: If it was blocking, the merge goes out with the problem.

choices.text: As blocking, or ask
choices.why: Right. Ask, and until then assume it must be dealt with.

choices.text: As a personal remark
choices.why: The lack of a label says nothing about intent.

choices.text: As a request to close the pull request
choices.why: Nothing in a comment implies that.

prompt: Ana's comment says an empty field still submits. Why is it not a comment about Bruno?
hint: Read what the sentence is about.

choices.text: It describes a line's behaviour
choices.why: Right. It names the code and what it does.

choices.text: Ana is his friend
choices.why: Friendship does not decide what a sentence is about.

choices.text: It was written politely
choices.why: Politeness is tone; the subject is the line.

choices.text: Reviewers are not allowed to criticise
choices.why: Criticising the code is the job.

prompt: A comment reads: Why is this here? How does the lesson suggest reading it?

choices.text: As an accusation, and defend the line
choices.why: If it was curiosity, the defence answers nothing asked.

choices.text: As a question, and answer it
choices.why: Right. You lose nothing if you were wrong.

choices.text: As a request to delete the line
choices.why: It asks why, not for removal.

choices.text: As something to ignore
choices.why: Every comment gets an answer.

prompt: A comment says: you always do this. What does the lesson suggest?
hint: This one really is about a person.

choices.text: Reply in the same tone on the thread
choices.why: That turns a bad comment into a public argument.

choices.text: Accept it; reviewers know best
choices.why: A comment about a person is a problem with the comment.

choices.text: Delete your pull request
choices.why: The change is not the problem.

choices.text: Raise it calmly, in private
choices.why: Right. With the person, or whoever runs the team.

prompt: Why does Bruno fix the blocking comment with a new commit instead of amending the old one?
hint: What does Ana need to re-read?

choices.text: amend is not allowed on branches
choices.why: It is allowed; it rewrites what was reviewed.

choices.text: New commits run the checks faster
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: So what changed is one commit
choices.why: Right. Ana reads only that, not everything again.

choices.text: Git refuses to push amended commits
choices.why: It needs a force push, which the lesson avoids.

prompt: Why answer every comment, even with just done?

choices.text: The hosting service requires it
choices.why: It does not; the reviewer needs it.

choices.text: To raise the comment count
choices.why: The count means nothing.

choices.text: Unanswered, it looks missed or ignored
choices.why: Right. The reviewer cannot tell which.

choices.text: So the merge button unlocks
choices.why: Replies do not unlock merging.

prompt: Bruno starts 32-heading-colour from main, not from 30-pickup-times. Why?
hint: What would the new branch carry otherwise?

choices.text: Branches can only start from main
choices.why: A branch can start from any commit.

choices.text: So it carries nothing of #31
choices.why: Right. #33 is reviewed and merged on its own.

choices.text: 30-pickup-times had been deleted
choices.why: It is still open for review.

choices.text: To avoid pushing twice
choices.why: It is pushed separately either way.

prompt: Bruno replies to the nit: I kept Order so it matches the heading. Is that acceptable?

choices.text: No; every comment must be applied
choices.why: Then there would be no difference between a nit and a blocker.

choices.text: No; he should close the thread silently
choices.why: Silence is the one thing to avoid.

choices.text: Only if Ana approves first
choices.why: The nit is his call regardless.

choices.text: Yes; a nit is his, and he gave a reason
choices.why: Right. Declining with a reason is what a nit allows.

prompt: Match each of Ana's comments to Bruno's reply.
hint: One reply answers nothing Ana asked.

pairs.left: Place order says more than Order
pairs.right: Kept Order to match the heading

prompt: Bruno's fix adds one attribute so the browser refuses an empty time: <input name="pickup" type="time" ___>
Which reply disagrees well with a request to use a list of times?
hint: It gives the reviewer something to weigh.

choices.text: I prefer the field.
choices.why: A preference with no reason; the thread goes round again.

choices.text: Fine, I will change it.
choices.why: Giving in without saying why he disagreed wastes his reasoning.

choices.text: Thirty options on a phone is slow. Your worry?
choices.why: Right. What he chose, why, and a question back.

choices.text: Lists are an outdated pattern.
choices.why: A claim with no link to this form or its users.

prompt: Two rounds of replies have not converged. What next?

choices.text: A longer third reply
choices.why: A third written round rarely settles it.

choices.text: Talk, then write the outcome down
choices.why: Right. A call, then one line on the thread.

choices.text: Merge without an approval
choices.why: That skips the review entirely.

choices.text: Close the pull request and start over
choices.why: The disagreement would follow.

prompt: Match each situation to how it is settled.
hint: One way of settling fits none.

pairs.right: Often cheapest to just do it

pairs.left: The same argument in every pull request

prompt: Three reviews in a row find a missing required. What is worth doing?

choices.text: Stop asking for reviews on forms
choices.why: The reviews are what found it.

choices.text: Add it to a checklist for the next form
choices.why: Right. The lesson is learnt once.

choices.text: Ask the reviewer to stop mentioning it
choices.why: The problem is the missing attribute.

choices.text: Nothing; it is a coincidence
choices.why: Three times is a pattern.

prompt: An author accepts every comment without question to avoid friction. What does the lesson say about that?

choices.text: It is the ideal review
choices.why: A reviewer can be wrong too.

choices.text: Only one person thought
choices.why: Right. Disagreeing with a reason is part of the job.

choices.text: It speeds up the merge
choices.why: Perhaps, at the cost of the reviewer's mistakes.

choices.text: It shows respect for seniority
choices.why: Respect includes saying when you see it differently.

prompt: Put Bruno's handling of the review in order.
hint: Replies come after the fixes they point at.
items: Commit the fix for the blocking one
trap: Replying Fixed before pushing points Ana at a commit she cannot see yet.

prompt: Which of these are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two are about commits, two about people.

choices.text: Fixes during review go in as new commits
choices.why: Yes. The reviewer reads only what changed.

choices.text: Experienced developers get no blocking comments
choices.why: Fewer, not zero.

choices.text: A short comment often reads harsher than meant
choices.why: Yes. Text loses tone.

choices.text: An out-of-scope change should be force-pushed away
choices.why: It leaves as a new commit, like any fix.
